starters.title: Reverse a restricted decreasing line
starters.question:
Let \(f(x)=7-2x\) for \(-1\le x<5\).

  1. Find the range of \(f\). [2]
  2. Find \(f^{-1}(x)\) and state its domain. [2]
  3. Find \(f^{-1}(-1)\). [1]
starters.solution:
1. The included end gives \(f(-1)=9\). The excluded end would give \(f(5)=-3\). The function decreases throughout, so the range is \((-3,9]\). [2]
  2. Rearranging \(y=7-2x\) gives \(x=(7-y)/2\). Thus \(f^{-1}(x)=(7-x)/2\) on \((-3,9]\). [2]
  3. \(f^{-1}(-1)=(7+1)/2=4\). [1]

starters.title: Reverse a fractional rule
starters.question:
Let \(g(x)=2+\dfrac5{x+1}\) for \(x>-1\).

  1. Find the range of \(g\). [2]
  2. Find \(g^{-1}(x)\) and state its domain. [3]
  3. Find the input \(x\) for which \(g^{-1}(x)=4\). [1]
starters.solution:
1. As \(x+1\) runs through all positive numbers, \(5/(x+1)\) does too. The range is \((2,\infty)\). [2]
  2. From \((y-2)(x+1)=5\), obtain \(g^{-1}(x)=-1+5/(x-2)\) with \(x>2\). Its domain is the original range. [3]
  3. Apply \(g\) to \(4\). The required input is \(g(4)=2+5/5=3\). [1]

starters.title: Recover a centre from a diameter
starters.question:
A circle has diameter \(AB\), where \(A=(-5,2)\) and \(B=(3,8)\).

  1. Find the length \(AB\). [2]
  2. Find the centre of the circle. [2]
  3. Find the squared radius. [1]
starters.solution:
1. The coordinate changes are \(8\) and \(6\). Thus \(AB=\sqrt{8^2+6^2}=10\). [2]
  2. The centre is the midpoint \(\left(\frac{-5+3}{2},\frac{2+8}{2}\right)=(-1,5)\). [2]
  3. The radius is \(5\), so its square is \(25\). [1]

starters.title: Locate a point equidistant from two ends
starters.question:
The point \(T\) lies on the \(y\)-axis and is equidistant from \(P(-3,2)\) and \(Q(5,4)\).

  1. Find the coordinates of \(T\). [3]
  2. Find the exact length \(TP\). [2]
starters.solution:
1. Write \(T=(0,t)\). Equate \(9+(t-2)^2\) and \(25+(t-4)^2\). After cancelling \(t^2\), \(4t=28\), so \(T=(0,7)\). [3]
  2. \(TP=\sqrt{3^2+5^2}=\sqrt{34}\). [2]

starters.title: Find a line, its intersection and its intercept area
starters.question:
The line \(l\) passes through \(A(-2,5)\) and \(B(4,2)\).

  1. Find an equation of \(l\). [3]
  2. Find the intersection of \(l\) with \(y=x+1\). [2]
  3. Find the area of the triangle bounded by \(l\) and the axes. [2]
starters.solution:
1. The gradient is \((2-5)/(4-(-2))=-\tfrac12\). Using \(A\) gives \(y-5=-\tfrac12(x+2)\), so \(l\) is \(y=4-\tfrac12x\). [3]
  2. From \(4-\tfrac12x=x+1\), find \(x=2\) and \(y=3\). The intersection is \((2,3)\). [2]
  3. The intercepts are \((8,0)\) and \((0,4)\). The area is \(\tfrac12(8)(4)=16\) square units. [2]

starters.title: Meet a perpendicular and find the exact distance
starters.question:
The line \(l\) has equation \(x+2y=8\). A line \(m\) goes through \(P(3,-2)\) perpendicular to \(l\).

  1. Find an equation of \(m\). [2]
  2. Find the intersection \(H\) of \(l\) and \(m\). [3]
  3. Find the exact length \(PH\). [2]
starters.solution:
1. The gradient of \(l\) is \(-\tfrac12\). The perpendicular through \(P\) is \(y+2=2(x-3)\), or \(y=2x-8\). [2]
  2. Substitute into \(x+2y=8\) to get \(5x=24\). The point is \(H=(\tfrac{24}5,\tfrac85)\). [3]
  3. The coordinate changes are \(\tfrac95\) and \(\tfrac{18}5\). Hence \(PH=9\sqrt5/5\). [2]

starters.title: A triangle and two central angles
starters.question:
A triangle has angles \(\alpha\), \(2\alpha\) and \(\frac{\pi}{5}\), all in radians.

  1. Find \(\alpha\) exactly.
  2. Express the largest angle of the triangle in degrees.
  3. A circle has a minor central angle equal to that largest angle. Find the reflex angle between the same radii, in radians.
starters.hint: First use the triangle angle sum. For the circle, the two central angles add to \(2\pi\).
starters.solution:
1. \(3\alpha+\frac{\pi}{5}=\pi\), so \(\alpha=\frac{4\pi}{15}\).

    The triangle's angles add to π.

  2. The largest angle is \(2\alpha=\frac{8\pi}{15}\); in degrees it is \((\frac{8\pi}{15})(\frac{180}{\pi})=96^\circ\).

    Check all three angle sizes before choosing the largest.

  3. The reflex angle is \(2\pi-\frac{8\pi}{15}=\frac{22\pi}{15}\text{ rad}\).

    The circular angles use a full-turn sum.
starters.marking:
• 1 method mark for the triangle angle equation.

  • 1 accuracy mark for α=\(\frac{4\pi}{15}\).

  • 1 method mark for converting the largest angle with \(\frac{180}{\pi}\).

  • 1 accuracy mark for 96°.

  • 1 accuracy mark for the reflex angle \(\frac{22\pi}{15}\).

starters.title: A pointer reverses
starters.question:
A pointer starts along a reference ray. It turns \(\frac{9\pi}{2}\) radians clockwise, then \(\frac{5\pi}{3}\) radians anticlockwise. Take anticlockwise as positive.

Find (a) its total angular travel, (b) its net signed rotation and (c) its final anticlockwise direction in \([0,2\pi)\). Give exact answers.
starters.hint: Add magnitudes for travel. Use signs for net rotation, then add enough complete turns to put the final direction in the stated interval.
starters.solution:
1. Total travel \(=\frac{9\pi}{2}+\frac{5\pi}{3}=\frac{37\pi}{6}\text{ rad}\).

    Both movements contribute to the travel.

  2. Net rotation \(=-\frac{9\pi}{2}+\frac{5\pi}{3}=-\frac{17\pi}{6}\text{ rad}\).

    The first turn is clockwise and negative.

  3. \(-\frac{17\pi}{6}+4\pi=\frac{7\pi}{6}\text{ rad}\).

    Adding one turn still gives a negative value; adding two produces the required final direction.
starters.marking:
• 1 method mark for adding both magnitudes.

  • 1 accuracy mark for \(\frac{37\pi}{6}\) total travel.

  • 1 method mark for a correctly signed sum.

  • 1 accuracy mark for −\(\frac{17\pi}{6}\) net rotation.

  • 1 accuracy mark for \(\frac{7\pi}{6}\) as the final direction.

starters.title: Three angles around a point
starters.question:
Three adjacent angles make a complete turn around a point. Their sizes are \((3x+0.2)\), \((2x+0.6)\) and \((x+0.4)\) radians.

Find \(x\) exactly in terms of \(\pi\), then find the smallest angle to 3 significant figures.
starters.hint: The three angles add to \(2\pi\). Find each angle before deciding which is smallest.
starters.solution:
1. \(6x+1.2=2\pi\), so \(x=\frac{\pi}{3}-0.2=\frac{\pi}{3}-\frac{1}{5}\).

    Collect the x-terms and constants.

  2. The three angles are \(\pi-0.4\), \(\frac{2\pi}{3}+0.2\), and \(\frac{\pi}{3}+0.2\).

    Substitute the exact value of x.

  3. The smallest is \(\frac{\pi}{3}+0.2=1.24719\ldots=1.25\text{ rad}\).

    Compare before rounding; all three angles are positive.
starters.marking:
• 1 method mark for the full-turn equation.

  • 1 accuracy mark for x=\(\frac{\pi}{3}\)−\(\frac{1}{5}\).

  • 1 method mark for comparing the substituted angles.

  • 1 accuracy mark for 1.25 rad.

starters.title: One angle, two arc lengths
starters.question:
A sector has radius \(r\text{ cm}\) and angle \(\theta\) radians. Its arc length is \(18\text{ cm}\). When the radius is increased by \(3\text{ cm}\), keeping the same angle, the arc length becomes \(22.5\text{ cm}\).

Find \(r\), \(\theta\) and the perimeter of the original sector.
starters.hint: Write one arc equation for each radius. Subtract them before finding the original perimeter.
starters.solution:
1. \(r\theta=18,\quad(r+3)\theta=22.5\).

    The same angle appears in both arc equations.

  2. \(3\theta=4.5\), so \(\theta=1.5\text{ rad}\).

    Subtract the two equations.

  3. \(r=\frac{18}{1.5}=12\text{ cm}\).

    Substitute the angle into the first equation.

  4. \(P=18+2(12)=42\text{ cm}\).

    Use the original arc and original radii.

  5. \((12+3)(1.5)=22.5\text{ cm}\).

    Check the changed sector condition.
starters.marking:
• 1 method mark for rθ=18.

  • 1 method mark for (r+3)θ=22.5.

  • 1 method mark for eliminating rθ.

  • 1 accuracy mark for θ=1.5.

  • 1 accuracy mark for r=12.

  • 1 accuracy mark for the original perimeter 42 cm.

starters.title: A rolling wheel returns part of the way
starters.question:
A wheel of radius \(24\text{ cm}\) rolls without slipping along a straight path. It makes \(2.5\) turns forward, then \(0.75\) turns backward.

Find, in metres, (a) the total distance travelled and (b) the net forward displacement from its starting position. Give exact answers.
starters.hint: Use radius 0.24 m. Add the turn counts for distance and subtract for displacement.
starters.solution:
1. \(r=0.24\text{ m}\), so one turn covers \(2\pi r=0.48\pi\text{ m}\).

    Convert the radius before calculating the requested metre distances.

  2. Total distance \(=(2.5+0.75)(0.48\pi)=1.56\pi=\frac{39\pi}{25}\text{ m}\).

    Both parts of the journey contribute to distance.

  3. Net forward displacement \(=(2.5-0.75)(0.48\pi)=0.84\pi=\frac{21\pi}{25}\text{ m}\).

    Backward travel reduces the final forward change in position.
starters.marking:
• 1 method mark for the correct circumference in metres.

  • 1 method mark for adding travel in both directions.

  • 1 accuracy mark for \(\frac{39\pi}{25}\) m.

  • 1 method mark for subtracting backward travel.

  • 1 accuracy mark for \(\frac{21\pi}{25}\) m.

starters.title: The perimeter increases after a cut
starters.question:
A minor sector of angle \(\alpha\) radians is removed from a disk of radius \(10\text{ cm}\). The perimeter of the remaining region is \(12\text{ cm}\) greater than the original circumference.

Find (a) \(\alpha\), (b) the length of the remaining arc and (c) the remaining perimeter. Give exact answers.
starters.hint: The cut removes an arc \(10\alpha\) and adds two straight edges of 10 cm each.
starters.solution:
1. Perimeter change \(=20-10\alpha=12\).

    Compare edges removed with edges added.

  2. \(10\alpha=8\), so \(\alpha=0.8\text{ rad}\).

    This lies between 0 and π, as required for a minor sector.

  3. Remaining arc \(=10(2\pi-0.8)=20\pi-8\text{ cm}\).

    The remaining region uses the major arc.

  4. Remaining perimeter \(=(20\pi-8)+20=20\pi+12\text{ cm}\).

    Add both cut edges and verify the stated increase.
starters.marking:
• 1 method mark for identifying the removed arc and two new radii.

  • 1 method mark for 20−10α=12.

  • 1 accuracy mark for α=0.8.

  • 1 method mark for the major angle 2π−α.

  • 1 accuracy mark for remaining arc 20π−8.

  • 1 accuracy mark for remaining perimeter 20π+12.

starters.title: Reconstruct and redesign
starters.question:
A proper sector has area \(96\text{ cm}^2\) and arc length \(16\) cm.

  1. Find its radius, angle and perimeter.
  2. The radius is kept fixed while the angle is increased by \(50\%\). Find the new area and new perimeter.

Give exact answers and show the formulas you use.
starters.hint: Use \(A=\frac12rs\). With fixed radius, increasing the angle by 50% multiplies the area and arc by 1.5, but leaves the two radii unchanged.
starters.solution:
1. \[r=\frac{2(96)}{16}=12\text{ cm}.\]

  2. \[\theta=\frac{16}{12}=\frac43\text{ rad},\qquad P=16+24=40\text{ cm}.\]

  3. \[\theta_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac32\times\frac43=2\text{ rad}.\]

  4. \[A_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac12(12)^2(2)=144\text{ cm}^2.\]

  5. \[P_{\mathrm{new}}=12(2)+2(12)=48\text{ cm}.\]

  6. Both angles are between 0 and \(2\pi\), so both sectors are valid.
starters.marking:
• Use A=rs/2 to obtain r=12 (2 marks).

  • Find θ=\(\frac{4}{3}\) and P=40 (2 marks).

  • Obtain the new angle 2 or correctly use the angle multiplier (1 mark).

  • Find new area 144 and perimeter 48 (2 marks).

starters.title: A minor-sector condition
starters.question:
A proper sector has perimeter \(38\) cm and area \(84\text{ cm}^2\).

  1. Find every pair \((r,\theta)\), with radius in cm and angle in radians.
  2. A design specification adds that the sector must be minor. State the radius of the sector that now remains.
starters.hint: First solve \(84=\frac12r(38-2r)\). For part 2, compare each angle with \(\pi\).
starters.solution:
1. \[r^2-19r+84=0\Rightarrow(r-7)(r-12)=0.\]

  2. \[r=7\Rightarrow\theta=\frac{38-14}{7}=\frac{24}{7},\qquad r=12\Rightarrow\theta=\frac{38-24}{12}=\frac76.\]

  3. Both angles are less than \(2\pi\), so both pairs satisfy the original description.

  4. Since \(\frac{24}{7}\gt \pi\), that sector is reflex. Since \(\frac{7}{6}\lt \pi\), the minor sector has radius \(12\) cm.
starters.marking:
• Form the area-perimeter equation and obtain r²−19r+84=0 (2 marks).

  • Solve for both radii 7 and 12 (1 mark).

  • Recover the two corresponding angles \(\frac{24}{7}\) and \(\frac{7}{6}\) (2 marks).

  • Check the proper-sector restrictions and correctly apply θ<π to select r=12 (2 marks).

starters.title: An allowed maximum and an excluded limit
starters.question:
A proper sector has fixed perimeter \(48\) cm and satisfies \(0\lt \theta\le\frac{4}{3}\).

  1. Express its area in terms of its radius \(r\), and determine the allowed interval of \(r\).
  2. Without differentiation, find its greatest area and the radius and angle at which it occurs.
  3. If the restriction becomes \(0\lt \theta\lt \frac{4}{3}\), decide whether the greatest area from part 2 is still attained.

Enter exact final values below; show the model, interval and completed square on paper.
starters.hint: Use \(\theta=\frac{48}{r}-2\) and \(A=24r-r^2\). The unrestricted vertex is at \(r=12\); check whether it belongs to the allowed interval.
starters.solution:
1. \[A=\frac12r(48-2r)=24r-r^2.\]

  2. \[\frac{48}{r}-2\le\frac43\Rightarrow\frac{48}{r}\le\frac{10}{3}\Rightarrow r\ge\frac{72}{5}.\]

  3. Also \(\theta\gt 0\) requires \(r\lt 24\). Thus \(\frac{72}{5}\le r\lt 24\).

  4. \[A=144-(r-12)^2.\]

  5. All allowed radii are greater than 12, so the square is smallest at the included endpoint \(r=\frac{72}{5}\).

  6. \[A_{\max}=144-\left(\frac{72}{5}-12\right)^2=144-\frac{144}{25}=\frac{3456}{25}\text{ cm}^2.\]

  7. \[\theta=\frac{48}{\frac{72}{5}}-2=\frac43\text{ rad}.\]

  8. Under the strict restriction, \(r\gt \frac{72}{5}\). The area is always less than \(\frac{3456}{25}\), although it can approach that value. The bound is no longer attained.
starters.marking:
• Build A=24r−r² (1 mark).

  • Translate both angle bounds to \(\frac{72}{5}\)≤r<24 (2 marks).

  • Complete the square and recognise that its vertex is excluded (2 marks).

  • Obtain the allowed endpoint radius, corresponding angle and greatest area (3 marks).

  • Explain non-attainment after the strict-bound change (1 mark).

starters.title: One chord, two segments
starters.question:
A chord \(AB\) lies in a circle of radius \(10\) cm and subtends the minor central angle \(\frac{2\pi}{3}\).

  1. Find \(AB\).
  2. Find the areas of both segments.
  3. Find the perimeter of the major segment. Give exact answers and show how each area and boundary is assembled.
starters.hint: Use the half-angle for the chord, the full minor angle for the triangle, and \(2\pi-\theta\) for the major arc.
starters.solution:
1. \(AB=2(10)\sin(\frac{\pi}{3})=10\sqrt3\) cm.

    The half-chord triangle has angle \(\frac{\pi}{3}\).

  2. \(A_{\rm sector}=\tfrac12(100)(\frac{2\pi}{3})=\frac{100\pi}{3}\), and \(A_{\triangle}=\tfrac12(100)\sin(\frac{2\pi}{3})=25\sqrt3\).

    Find the two component areas.

  3. \(A_{\rm minor}=\frac{100\pi}{3}-25\sqrt3\text{ cm}^2\).

    The minor segment is sector minus triangle.

  4. \(A_{\rm major}=100\pi-A_{\rm minor}=\frac{200\pi}{3}+25\sqrt3\text{ cm}^2\).

    Use the rest of the disk.

  5. \(P_{\rm major}=10(\frac{4\pi}{3})+10\sqrt3=\frac{40\pi}{3}+10\sqrt3\) cm.

    The major boundary is the long arc plus the shared chord.
starters.marking:
• 2 marks: use the half-angle correctly and obtain the chord.

  • 2 marks: identify sector minus triangle and obtain the minor area.

  • 2 marks: subtract the minor area from the disk and obtain the major area.

  • 2 marks: use the major arc plus chord and obtain the perimeter.

starters.title: A chord measured on a large circle
starters.question:
A circle has radius \(20\) cm and a chord of length \(24\) cm.

  1. Find the perpendicular distance from the centre to the chord.
  2. Find the minor central angle.
  3. Find the area of the minor segment and the perimeter of the major segment. Give the distance exactly and all other numerical answers to 3 significant figures. Keep your angle unrounded during the calculation.
starters.hint: The half-chord is \(12\) cm. The triangle area can be calculated directly as \(\tfrac12\times24\times d\).
starters.solution:
1. \(d=\sqrt{20^2-12^2}=16\) cm.

    Use the half-chord triangle.

  2. \(\theta=2\arcsin(\frac{12}{20})=1.287002\ldots\approx1.29\) rad.

    Save the full value of \(\theta\).

  3. \(A_{\triangle}=\tfrac12(24)(16)=192\text{ cm}^2\).

    The chord is a base and the perpendicular distance is its height.

  4. \(A_{\rm minor}=200\theta-192=65.4004\ldots\approx65.4\text{ cm}^2\).

    Subtract from the minor sector.

  5. \(P_{\rm major}=20(2\pi-\theta)+24=123.9236\ldots\approx124\) cm.

    Add the long arc and the chord.
starters.marking:
• 2 marks: a correct half-chord Pythagoras method and distance.

  • 2 marks: a correct inverse-ratio method and radian central angle.

  • 2 marks: correct sector-minus-triangle assembly and minor area.

  • 2 marks: correct major-arc-plus-chord assembly and rounded perimeter.

starters.title: Reconstruct a circular cap
starters.question:
A minor circular cap has a straight chord \(12\) cm long. Its greatest perpendicular height above the chord is \(2\) cm.

  1. Form an equation and find the circle's radius.
  2. Find the minor central angle.
  3. Find the cap's area and perimeter. Give the radius exactly and the other answers to 3 significant figures.
starters.hint: Use \(r^2=(r-2)^2+6^2\). After finding \(r\), find the distance to the chord and the half-angle.
starters.solution:
1. \(r^2=(r-2)^2+36=r^2-4r+40\).

    The centre-to-chord distance is \(r-2\).

  2. \(4r=40\), so \(r=10\) cm and \(d=8\) cm.

    Solve and check the cap height is smaller than the radius.

  3. \(\theta=2\arccos(\frac{8}{10})=1.287002\ldots\approx1.29\) rad.

    Use the half-angle cosine ratio.

  4. \(A=\tfrac12(10^2)\theta-\tfrac12(12)(8)=100\arccos(\frac{4}{5})-48\approx16.4\text{ cm}^2\).

    Remove the triangle from the sector.

  5. \(P=10\theta+12=20\arccos(\frac{4}{5})+12\approx24.9\) cm.

    Only the chord and minor arc form the cap boundary.
starters.marking:
• 3 marks: construct the right-triangle equation, solve it and obtain the valid radius.

  • 2 marks: obtain the minor central angle by an inverse ratio.

  • 2 marks: assemble and calculate the cap area.

  • 2 marks: assemble and calculate the cap perimeter.

starters.title: Recover a strip and complete its ring
starters.question:
An annular sector has radial width \(5\) cm, angle \(0.8\) rad and area \(50\text{ cm}^2\).

  1. Find both radii.
  2. Find its complete perimeter.
  3. Find the area and total boundary length of the complete annulus with the same radii. Give exact answers, and explain the change in boundary in part
  4. .
starters.hint: Obtain \(R+r\) from the area and known width. A full ring has two circles as its boundary and no radial ends.
starters.solution:
1. \(50=\tfrac12(R^2-r^2)(0.8)\), so \(R^2-r^2=125\).

    Rearrange the area equation.

  2. \((R-r)(R+r)=125\) and \(R-r=5\), giving \(R+r=25\).

    Factor the difference of squares.

  3. \(R=15\), \(r=10\) cm; \(P=25(0.8)+2(5)=30\) cm.

    Recover the radii and count all four sector edges.

  4. \(A_{\rm ring}=\pi(225-100)=125\pi\text{ cm}^2\).

    Remove the inner disk from the outer disk.

  5. \(P_{\rm ring}=2\pi(15)+2\pi(10)=50\pi\) cm.

    The radial ends are internal when the ring closes.
starters.marking:
• 2 marks: use the area and width to obtain the sum of the radii.

  • 2 marks: solve for the correct positive radii and obtain the sector perimeter.

  • 2 marks: calculate the full annulus area.

  • 2 marks: include both circular boundaries, exclude radial ends and obtain the boundary length.

starters.title: Same perimeter, different area
starters.question:
Two designs begin with squares of side \(12\) cm. Design A removes one internal quadrant of radius \(8\) cm centred at a corner. Design B removes two non-overlapping internal quadrants, of radii \(5\) cm and \(3\) cm, centred at opposite corners.

  1. Find each remaining area.
  2. Show that the two remaining regions have the same perimeter and find it.
  3. Find how much larger B's area is, and explain why equal perimeter does not force equal area.
starters.hint: The removed straight lengths and added arc lengths depend on the radii. The removed areas depend on their squares.
starters.solution:
1. \(A_A=144-\frac{\pi(8^2)}{4}=144-16\pi\text{ cm}^2\).

    Remove one quarter-disk.

  2. \(A_B=144-\frac{\pi(5^2+3^2)}{4}=144-\frac{17\pi}{2}\text{ cm}^2\).

    Add the two separate cut-out areas.

  3. \(P_A=48-2(8)+\frac{8\pi}{2}=32+4\pi\) cm.

    Replace two straight pieces with one quadrant arc.

  4. \(P_B=48-2(5+3)+\frac{(5+3)\pi}{2}=32+4\pi\) cm.

    The sum of the two radii equals 8, so the boundary total is the same.

  5. \(A_B-A_A=16\pi-\frac{17\pi}{2}=\frac{15\pi}{2}\text{ cm}^2\).

    The squares do not add in the same way: \(5^2+3^2\ne8^2\).
starters.marking:
• 2 marks: obtain the area of design A.

  • 2 marks: obtain the area of design B.

  • 3 marks: correctly account for both boundary constructions and show the common perimeter.

  • 2 marks: obtain the area difference and explain the role of squared radii.

starters.title: A lens with a measured centre distance
starters.question:
Two disks each have radius \(10\) cm and their centres are \(12\) cm apart. Their circles meet at \(A\) and \(B\).

  1. Find the common chord \(AB\) and the minor angle it subtends at either centre.
  2. Find the area and perimeter of the overlap.
  3. Find the union area. Give exact answers; inverse-trigonometric expressions are acceptable.
starters.hint: The chord is \(6\) cm from either centre. Each small centre–chord triangle has base \(AB\) and perpendicular height \(6\).
starters.solution:
1. \(AM=\sqrt{10^2-6^2}=8\), so \(AB=16\) cm.

    The midpoint of the chord is also the midpoint of the line of centres.

  2. \(\theta=2\arccos(\frac{6}{10})=2\arccos(\frac{3}{5})\).

    Recover the acute half-angle.

  3. One sector has area \(50\theta\), while its triangle has area \(\tfrac12(16)(6)=48\).

    Separate the sector and triangle before forming a segment.

  4. \(A_{\rm overlap}=2(50\theta-48)=200\arccos(\frac{3}{5})-96\text{ cm}^2\).

    The lens contains two congruent segments.

  5. \(P_{\rm overlap}=2(10)\theta=40\arccos(\frac{3}{5})\) cm.

    The common chord is internal.

  6. \(A_{\rm union}=200\pi-A_{\rm overlap}=200\pi-200\arccos(\frac{3}{5})+96\text{ cm}^2\).

    Count the overlap only once in the union.
starters.marking:
• 2 marks: use the centre-to-chord right triangle and obtain the common chord.

  • 2 marks: derive the minor angle using an inverse ratio.

  • 3 marks: assemble two segment areas and obtain the overlap area.

  • 1 mark: use the two arcs for the overlap perimeter.

  • 2 marks: apply inclusion–exclusion and obtain the union area.

starters.title: Does a largest stadium exist?
starters.question:
A stadium consists of a rectangle of length \(\ell>0\) and width \(2r\), with an external semicircle of radius \(r\) attached along each of the two sides of length \(2r\). Its outside perimeter is \(36\) cm, and \(r\geq3\) cm.

  1. Express \(\ell\) in terms of \(r\) and determine the permitted values of \(r\).
  2. Express the area \(A\) in terms of \(r\), then complete the square.
  3. Find the least area, the least upper bound for the area, and whether the upper bound is attained. Do not use calculus. Write the algebra and argument on paper before checking the results.
starters.hint: Use \(\ell=18-\pi r\). In the permitted interval, \(r\) approaches but never reaches the vertex of the area quadratic.
starters.solution:
1. \(2\ell+2\pi r=36\), so \(\ell=18-\pi r\). Thus \(3\leq r<\frac{18}{\pi}\).

    Combine the given lower bound with the positive rectangle-length condition.

  2. \(A=2r\ell+\pi r^2=36r-\pi r^2\).

    The two semicircles together have disk area.

  3. \(A=\frac{324}{\pi}-\pi(r-\frac{18}{\pi})^2\).

    Complete the square.

  4. As \(r\) increases from 3 towards \(\frac{18}{\pi}\), the positive distance \(\frac{18}{\pi}-r\) decreases. Therefore its square decreases and \(A\) increases.

    This proves the ordering of areas without differentiating.

  5. The least area is at \(r=3\): \(A_{\min}=108-9\pi\text{ cm}^2\).

    The lower endpoint is allowed, so this value is attained.

  6. \(A<\frac{324}{\pi}\text{ cm}^2\). The upper bound is approached but not attained, because equality needs \(r=\frac{18}{\pi}\) and \(\ell=0\).

    Distinguish an upper bound from an allowed maximum.
starters.marking:
• 2 marks: derive the rectangle-length expression and correct radius restrictions.

  • 2 marks: derive the area quadratic.

  • 2 marks: complete the square correctly.

  • 2 marks: justify and calculate the attained minimum.

  • 2 marks: identify the upper bound and explain why it is not attained.
